## Problem`GetQueueStatsAsync` loads the **entire `SliceJobs` table four times** — once per status — with change tracking on, and materializes every row including eight `TEXT` columns, purely to call `.Count` on each list. It is called on every slice-job submission and inside per-engine loops.`src/slicer/Farm.Slicer.Module/Services/DbSlicerJobQueue.cs:109-127`## Evidence```csharppublic async Task<SlicerQueueStats> GetQueueStatsAsync(SlicerEngineType? engine = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default){    IReadOnlyList<SliceJob> queued = await _repo.GetByStatusAsync(SliceJobStatus.Queued, limit: null, ct: cancellationToken);    IReadOnlyList<SliceJob> processing = await _repo.GetByStatusAsync(SliceJobStatus.Processing, limit: null, ct: cancellationToken);    IReadOnlyList<SliceJob> completed = await _repo.GetByStatusAsync(SliceJobStatus.Completed, limit: null, ct: cancellationToken);    IReadOnlyList<SliceJob> failed = await _repo.GetByStatusAsync(SliceJobStatus.Failed, limit: null, ct: cancellationToken);    return new SlicerQueueStats    {        Engine = engine ?? SlicerEngineType.OrcaSlicer,        QueuedJobs = queued.Count,        ProcessingJobs = processing.Count,        CompletedJobs = completed.Count,        FailedJobs = failed.Count,        ...    };}````limit: null` means no `Take` is applied, so each call is an unbounded `SELECT *` — `src/slicer/Farm.Slicer.Module/Data/Repositories/EfSliceJobRepository.cs:48-60`:```csharppublic async Task<IReadOnlyList<SliceJob>> GetByStatusAsync(string status, int? limit = null, CancellationToken ct = default){    IQueryable<SliceJob> query = _db.SliceJobs        .Where(j => j.Status == status)        .OrderByDescending(j => j.QueuedAt);    if (limit.HasValue) { query = query.Take(limit.Value); }    return await query.ToListAsync(ct);   // no AsNoTracking}```The entity is wide. `src/slicer/Farm.Slicer.Module/Data/Configurations/SliceJobConfiguration.cs:31-52` declares **eight `TEXT` columns**, three of which are full resolved OrcaSlicer profile snapshots:```csharpbuilder.Property(j => j.SlicerProfileJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.RequiredCapabilitiesJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.ErrorMessage).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.ExtruderFilamentProfileNamesJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.ModelFileUrlsJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.MachineProfileJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.ProcessProfileJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");builder.Property(j => j.FilamentProfileJson).HasColumnType("TEXT");```Call sites in `src/slicer/Farm.Slicer.Module/Services/SlicerOrchestrator.cs`:| Line | Context ||---|---|| 45 | idempotent re-submission || 113 | **every** job submission || 231 | inside `foreach` over engine catalog || 283 | inside `foreach (SlicerEngineType engineType in _engineCatalog.Keys)` || 364 | inside `foreach` over engine catalog || 401 | health / connectivity probe |`Completed` and `Failed` rows are never pruned by this path, so the scanned volume grows monotonically with slice history. There *is* already an index to support a cheap aggregate — `SliceJobConfiguration.cs:63`: `builder.HasIndex(j => j.Status)`.## Proposed fixReplace the four materializing queries with a single grouped aggregate that never leaves SQL, with `AsNoTracking()`:```csharpDictionary<string, int> counts = await db.SliceJobs    .AsNoTracking()    .GroupBy(j => j.Status)    .Select(g => new { Status = g.Key, Count = g.Count() })    .ToDictionaryAsync(x => x.Status, x => x.Count, ct);```**Rejected approach — do not do this:** naively hoisting one global count out of the per-engine loops. Reviewer flagged this as a correctness hazard. The `engine` parameter is currently accepted but *never used to filter* — it is only stamped onto the result (`Engine = engine ?? SlicerEngineType.OrcaSlicer`), while `_engineCatalog` genuinely holds more than one engine (`SlicerOrchestrator.cs:498` OrcaSlicer, `:503` PrusaSlicer). So today's per-engine numbers are already wrong, and a global hoist would cement that bug. **Group by normalized engine AND status**, define the fallback semantics for legacy rows with no engine recorded, then project per engine.## Expected impactBackend **throughput and memory**. Converts an unbounded row + large-`TEXT` transfer — repeated 4× per call and once per engine per loop iteration — into a single index-backed aggregate. This is on the slice submission path, so it is user-visible latency for operators submitting slice jobs, and the regression worsens over time as slice history accumulates. Magnitude scales with `SliceJobs` row count and stored profile-JSON size; unquantified until measured (see below).## Effort**S/M** — the query rewrite is small, but doing it correctly requires fixing the per-engine grouping and defining legacy-row fallback semantics, plus tests.## How to verify1. Seed a slicer database with a realistic history (e.g. 10k `Completed`/`Failed` `SliceJob` rows carrying representative `MachineProfileJson`/`ProcessProfileJson`/`FilamentProfileJson` payloads).2. Capture the baseline: enable EF Core command logging (or `ToQueryString()`), and record both **query count** and **bytes returned** for one `POST` slice submission.3. Apply the fix and re-measure. Expected: 4 unbounded `SELECT *` per engine collapse to 1 aggregate; returned bytes drop to a handful of rows.4. Assert wall-clock time of `GetQueueStatsAsync` before/after at that row count.5. Add a regression test asserting per-engine counts are correct when both OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer jobs exist — this must fail on today's code.## RiskModerate. `SlicerQueueStats` feeds submission responses, engine status, and health checks. The per-engine correctness fix is a **behavior change** — current callers receive engine-agnostic numbers mislabeled per engine. Any consumer that has adapted to the wrong values will see different output. Legacy rows without a recorded engine need explicit fallback semantics.## ReviewRubber-duck verdict: **FILE**.> The cost is real and on submission, engine-list, and health paths; four tracked full-row scans over large JSON columns are indefensible as history grows. However, grouping only by status and hoisting global counts would cement an existing correctness defect: callers expect engine-specific queue depths, and the catalog contains both OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer. Query once grouped by normalized engine **and** status, define legacy-row fallback semantics, then map results per engine. With tests, effort is S/M rather than S.Implementer: heed the correctness caveat. Do **not** ship a status-only global count.
